doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Armstrong's and Bix's limitations as part of their expression
summary: Cullum argues that self-taught players' limitations shape their style and make them speak emotionally; he feels he knew Bix.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And what does that constitute? I mean if people are telling a story, as Mat Domber said, there’s going to be an emotional response to it I think he said this morning. Is it possible to pin down, what is that? What makes that happen?

Well I think it’s a variety of things that create an emotional response. If you’ve got Armstrong, playing with a lot of passion and relatively few notes, and not unlimited technique. Now he could play anything he could think. But the whole system of his brain and his self-taught technique meant that his ideas were shaped in a certain way and the limitations become part of the style. So this is really a critical thing. This is really, really important. And that is the limitations are a very critical and important part of the style. So that’s one of the things that when you hear Louis you say you’re hearing his limitations as well as all his technique, which was vast.

Well for the time. In other words, the point is, you want this: enough technique to be able to express the idea. That’s all the technique that’s needed, to have the idea come out cleanly, beautifully. Here’s the idea. And here it is. And that’s all the technique you need for that idea. You don’t need more.
But a lot of people nowadays have more technique than they do ideas.

Well that’s okay. If you have more technique than you have ideas then it’s a bunch of wasted stuff that’s just in there for the sake of the technique. And just to have music just for the sake of the technique, then I think it’s a mistake. I think you’ve missed the boat, missed the point. And that’s one of the reason that we’re so fascinated by these self- taught musicians is that it is easier to sense their limitations and so you understand what they’re having to say. They talk to you. They speak to you. You feel what they’re saying to you. It becomes this emotional reaction to what they’re saying to you. You become one with them. Like I feel like I knew Bix Beiderbecke personally and he died in 1931. And I wasn’t born until 1941. I feel like I knew that guy. I listen to those things and I feel that I shook his hand, and you know, embraced him and knew him personally. You know it’s interesting.

I really like the way you put that. I never quite thought about a person’s limitations and how it shaped what they could play. But I know what you mean and Bix’s playing seems to look like his pictures too, the photographs of him. I just think he had this sort of vulnerable look to him that you could hear it in his music.

Yeah you could hear a certain kind of melancholy, a little pain or something that’s in there. And the more you listen — now you don’t hear it at first — but the more you listen to Beiderbecke you hear these little nuances, subtle things. But yeah, the thing about the limitations is sort of profound I think. I think it’s very important.
